name: Bacon's blindness to the leading science of his own day
plain_explanation: Despite being deeply interested in science and having a generally scientific outlook, Bacon missed or ignored much of the best actual scientific work being done around him: he rejected the Copernican theory, seems not to have known Kepler's New Astronomy (1609) despite having no excuse not to, missed the work of Vesalius on anatomy and Gilbert on magnetism, and even seems to have been unaware of the work of his own physician, William Harvey, on the circulation of the blood.
precise_definition: Russell's summary: 'Although science was what interested Bacon, and although his general outlook was scientific, he missed most of what was being done in science in his day,' rejecting Copernicus, apparently ignorant of Kepler, Vesalius, Gilbert, and even Harvey -- who, as Bacon's own physician, said Bacon 'writes philosophy like a Lord Chancellor.'
why_it_mattered: It qualifies Bacon's reputation as a prophet of science: his importance lies in his general methodological advocacy for empirical, inductive science rather than in any engagement with or contribution to the concrete scientific advances of his own era.
historical_origin: A biographical and intellectual limitation Russell attributes partly to Bacon's preoccupation with 'worldly success.'
examples: Apparent ignorance of Kepler's New Astronomy (1609), Vesalius's anatomy, Gilbert's work on magnetism, and Harvey's discovery of the circulation of the blood
